items.title: X-ray stopwatch can measure durations of just attoseconds
items.summary: The duration of short ångström-wavelength X-ray pulses, which lasted merely 170 attoseconds, has finally been measured accurately. The optical system designed for precision pulse duration metrology can be used as a ‘stopwatch’ to measure the rapid motion of electrons inside atoms and molecules, too.

items.title: Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says
items.summary: Some countries are introducing sweeping social-media bans for young people, but the impact of screen time is still under investigation.

items.title: ‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science
items.summary: Researchers hope that US lawmakers will push back against the Trump administration’s science policies — but there are limits to what Congress can do.

items.title: How a once-controversial idea is advancing understanding of Parkinson’s disease
items.summary: The disease is thought to be divided into two subtypes, depending on where it originates in the body — the gut or the brain.

items.title: Rise of Germanic and Celtic languages is written in ancient DNA
items.summary: Thousands of genome sequences identify human migrations that might have spread early forms of these tongues around Europe.

items.title: AI agents enter the ‘wet lab’
items.summary: An AI system coordinates laboratory instruments to conduct multi-step molecular-biology experiments with limited human intervention.

items.title: How the brain protects itself from Parkinson’s disease
items.summary: Brains are resilient. Harnessing their self-protective mechanisms might help to prevent or slow the progression of this neurodegenerative condition.

items.summary: Enjoy the month’s best science images. Plus, an outbreak of anthrax in African hippos and the places where biodiversity drops after humans leave.

items.title: Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease
items.summary: Most Parkinson’s therapies aim to reduce the motor-control symptoms that the disease triggers. But stem-cell transplants in the brain could alter the disease at a more fundamental level.

items.title: Progress accelerates in Parkinson’s treatments
items.summary: Researchers are reporting encouraging results for a disease that affects millions of people worldwide.

items.title: Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them
items.summary: It might seem counterproductive to put more people in nature, but sometimes human activity nurtures biodiversity.

items.title: See a tardigrade shed its skin — October’s best science images
items.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

items.title: Fruit, flies and getting frisky: how food odours trigger sexual arousal
items.summary: Males of a Drosophila species that thrives on a particular fruit need the smell of food to begin courtship. This environmental cue acts on defined mating circuits in the brain.

items.title: Six highlights from Parkinson’s disease research
items.summary: Targeting a new network, addressing gait issues and other advances from recent studies.

items.title: Cutting-edge technique uncovers how the spine’s shock absorbers bear load
items.summary: An exciting imaging approach reveals how discs of soft tissue in the spine respond to compressive force at the micrometre and nanometre scales.

items.title: Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains
items.summary: A clinical trial in three people tested a combination of gene-laden viruses and a drug.

items.title: A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers
items.summary: The process of making protein from RNA can go awry in cancer cells. This malfunction might be harnessed to create an effective gene-therapy tool that targets tumours.

items.title: Faint exoplanets detected using computational approach to remove glare from stars
items.summary: An image-processing framework for detecting exoplanets directly has been developed. The technique overcomes the telescope-stability barrier that has limited previous methods, reveals fainter exoplanets than other approaches can detect and could make imaging exo-Earths easier for future observatories.

items.title: People’s social networks can be unintentionally reshaped during randomized interventions
items.summary: A re-examination of a randomized controlled trial for a health-advice intervention reveals ripple effects and altered relationships in communities in rural Honduras.

items.title: Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease
items.summary: Neuroscientists are developing a new type of brain implant that will decode every movement and symptom of people with this neurodegenerative condition, seeking better ways to ease symptoms.

items.title: Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread
items.summary: The latest cases, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, come as the country grapples with ongoing Ebola and cholera outbreaks.

items.title: When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn
items.summary: For decades, conservation has worried about the risks of too many people. In some places, depopulation is the real threat.

items.title: Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?
items.summary: Researchers and advocates point to pollutants as a trigger for the neurodegenerative condition.

items.title: Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys
items.summary: After decades of work, researchers have begun trialling transplants of dopamine neurons into people with the neurodegenerative disease — with early signs of success.

items.title: Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories
items.summary: Scientists have yet to reveal how the human brain produces the subjective experience we perceive as consciousness, but research has pushed the field in exciting directions.

items.title: Infrared image detectors grown directly on read-out chips
items.summary: A film of lead sulfide — an infrared-sensitive semiconductor — has been grown directly on a circuit that can read out the material’s electrical signal through an approach called monolithic in situ integration. This brings material growth and electronic integration together into a single step. The resulting image sensor shows high sensitivity for infrared wavelengths.

items.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
items.summary: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.
